body:
Every humus application is a bedrock.App, and the root package’s humus.App is the lifecycle every humus app type is built on. It reads its settings, listens for signals, builds its telemetry and the user’s dependencies, runs one or more Services, shuts them down within a grace period, releases what was built, shuts its telemetry down and turns the outcome into an exit status.
Most applications will not use humus.App directly. Each runtime package — REST, gRPC, jobs, queues — provides an App of its own, built on humus.App with that package’s defaults, and that is the API most users touch. Using humus.App directly, for example to run a REST API and a gRPC service in one process, is the advanced path. Read this page before taking it; read it, too, to understand what the App a runtime package builds for you does.
Telemetry is part of the lifecycle: the App builds it before Init, logs through it, and shuts it down last. See Telemetry below, and the Telemetry page for what a service does with it. Health is not part of the lifecycle yet. It is added by Proposal: health monitors and probes, which integrates it with the lifecycle when it lands.
The design behind everything on this page is in Proposal: the humus App lifecycle, and the telemetry integration is in Proposal: OpenTelemetry without globals, Revision 2.
App An App has five fields:
Field Required Meaning Host yes the network and filesystem the App runs on: humus.OSHost() in main, and a Host the test controls in a test ShutdownGracePeriod yes, unless HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD is set the grace period when HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD is not set. It must be positive, so the zero value fails startup DrainDelay no the drain delay when HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY is not set: the pause between shutdown starting and Shutdown being called on the Services. It must not be negative; zero means no pause Telemetry yes the telemetry.Builder that builds the App’s telemetry: the end user’s own Builder in main, and telemetry.NoopBuilder or the Builder of humustest’s recorder, humustest.Telemetry, in tests Init yes builds the App’s dependencies and returns the Services to run Its main is one call to bedrock.Main, the only place a humus program touches the real process:
bedrock.Main(humus.App{ Host: humus.OSHost(), ShutdownGracePeriod: 30 * time.Second, // when HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD is not set DrainDelay: 5 * time.Second, // when HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY is not set Telemetry: buildTelemetry, Init: Init, }) buildTelemetry is the end user’s Builder. It starts from the telemetry package’s defaults, which write log records to standard output, and names the service:
func buildTelemetry(ctx context.Context, p bedrock.Process, dial telemetry.Dialer) (telemetry.SDK, error) { s := telemetry.DefaultSettings() s.ServiceName = "greeter" return telemetry.New(ctx, s, dial, p.Stdout) } ShutdownGracePeriod and DrainDelay are defaults: an operator overrides either through its variable without a rebuild. humus has no default grace period of its own, so an App sets ShutdownGracePeriod unless its environment always sets the variable; a DrainDelay left at zero means no pause. How long to pause and how long to allow for shutdown depend on the kind of App — a REST or gRPC App needs time for a load balancer to stop sending it connections, and a job does not — so each runtime package’s App sets its own.
Service A Service is a long-running part of an App: an HTTP server, a gRPC server, a queue consumer or a job. It has two methods, Serve and Shutdown, and the App gives it two shutdown signals, at different times:
Serve’s context is done as soon as the App starts shutting down, before the drain delay. Shutdown is called after the drain delay, with the grace period as its context’s deadline. A Service may stop on the first, as a job or a queue consumer does. Or it may keep serving until the second, as an HTTP, gRPC or health Service does, so that a load balancer still draining connections towards it is answered. This Service keeps serving until Shutdown:
type server struct { out io.Writer ready chan struct{} stopped chan struct{} } func newServer(out io.Writer) *server { return &server{ out: out, ready: make(chan struct{}), stopped: make(chan struct{}), } } func (s *server) Serve(ctx context.Context) error { _, err := fmt.Fprintln(s.out, "serve: serving") close(s.ready) if err != nil { return err } <-s.stopped return nil } func (s *server) Shutdown(ctx context.Context) error { close(s.stopped) _, err := fmt.Fprintln(s.out, "shutdown: stopped serving") return err } Closing ready tells the example that runs it when it is serving. Serve returns nil when Shutdown stopped it or when it finished on its own. Any Service returning from Serve ends the App, so a job is just a Service that returns, and an App is never partly up. Shutdown is called on every Service, including one whose Serve has already returned, so it must be safe to call then. If its context is done before the Service has stopped, Shutdown stops it at once and returns an error that wraps the context’s error.
Host A Host is what humus hands an App beyond its process: Listen, Dial and a filesystem, FS. Every field is required. In main an App runs on humus.OSHost(), which is net.Listen, a net.Dialer’s DialContext, and an FS that calls package os directly. In a test it runs on a Host whose listeners, dialler and filesystem the test controls, so that a whole App runs without touching the real host.
Host is meant for user code as well as for humus. Hand Host.Dial to a client that takes a dial function, such as pgx’s DialFunc, and open files through Host.FS rather than through package os.
Why FS hands out *os.File FS names files by OS path and opens them as *os.File, rather than through an in-memory filesystem:
Libraries that need a real file or a path keep working in a test: SQLite drivers, archive libraries, programs started with os/exec. There is no fake filesystem to build and keep in line with the real one. It is a one-way decision. An *os.File is always an OS handle, so moving to an in-memory filesystem later would change every signature. OSHost’s FS is not os.OpenRoot("/"), because an os.Root refuses to follow absolute symbolic links even when it is rooted at /, and paths on a real host routinely pass through them.
What it costs a test: the rule is that it opens no file outside its own temporary directory; it cannot make a write fail with a full disk, so code that needs that test puts an io.Writer seam in its own code; and file modification times are real under synctest, so code that compares ModTime() with time.Now() needs Chtimes in its tests.
Setup and OnStop Init is given a *humus.Setup holding the bedrock.Process the App is run with, the App’s Host and its telemetry, Setup.Telemetry. Init reads its configuration from Setup.Process, builds its dependencies on Setup.Host, takes their tracers, meters and loggers from Setup.Telemetry, and returns the Services to run. Its context is done when the App receives an interrupt or SIGTERM, so a slow Init, such as one retrying a database connection, is cancelled by a signal.
Setup.OnStop registers a function that releases something Init built. The functions work like t.Cleanup: they run in reverse order of registration once every Service has stopped, and they run when Init fails partway through too. So register each release as soon as the thing it releases is built:
func Init(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { out := s.Process.Stdout s.OnStop(func(context.Context) error { _, err := fmt.Fprintln(out, "on stop: close the cache") return err }) s.OnStop(func(context.Context) error { _, err := fmt.Fprintln(out, "on stop: close the queue") return err }) if _, err := config.Env(s.Process.Environment, "DATABASE_URL").Read(ctx); err != nil { return nil, err // exit 78: init: config DATABASE_URL: not found } return []humus.Service{newServer(out)}, nil } Run without DATABASE_URL, this App closes the queue and then the cache, logs init: config DATABASE_URL: not found at ERROR through its telemetry, and exits 78.
The OnStop functions share the grace period with the Services’ Shutdown: the context each is given is done when the grace period runs out.
What Run does, in order Reads the lifecycle’s settings from the process’s environment, defaulting each to its App field. A malformed one, or a bad default, exits 78 before the App listens for signals, and Init is never called. Listens for an interrupt and SIGTERM through the process’s NotifyContext, before the telemetry and Init, so a signal during a slow Builder or a slow Init cancels it. Builds the telemetry by calling App.Telemetry. If it fails, Init is never called, and the App exits 78 when a *config.Error is in the error chain, or 1 otherwise. Sets OpenTelemetry’s process-wide error handler, which writes each export error to standard error. Calls Init. If it fails, runs the OnStop functions registered so far, within the grace period, and exits 78 when a *config.Error is in Init’s error chain, or 1 otherwise. Calls Serve on every Service concurrently, and logs serving. Waits for a signal, or for the first Service to return. Stops listening for signals, so that a second interrupt or SIGTERM takes its default action and ends the process at once, cancels the context passed to Serve, and logs shutting down. Waits the drain delay: HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY, defaulting to App.DrainDelay. Calls Shutdown on every Service concurrently, waits for every Serve to return, and then runs the OnStop functions in reverse order of registration. All of this happens within one grace period, HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD, which starts after the drain delay. Then it logs stopped. Shuts the telemetry down. Returns the exit status. An Init that returns no Services ends the App at once, without a drain delay, as there is nothing to drain. A cancelled root context still gets a graceful shutdown: the grace period keeps the context’s values but not its cancellation. Every failure is the cause of the exit status. Once the telemetry is built, each failure is logged through it, one record per error; before that, it is written to standard error, one line per error. The lifecycle never recovers a panic.
Telemetry App.Telemetry is the App’s telemetry.Builder, and it is required. In main it is the end user’s own Builder, such as buildTelemetry above, which sources telemetry.Settings however it likes and calls telemetry.New. In a test it is telemetry.NoopBuilder, or the Builder of humustest’s recorder, humustest.Telemetry, when the test asserts on what the App emits. Telemetry explains how to write the Builder, what the defaults are, the console log format, and how logs get their trace context.
Telemetry is built after NotifyContext and before Init. Run calls App.Telemetry with the context that a signal cancels, the Process, and the Host’s Dial, so the OTLP exporters reach the collector through the Host. A Builder that runs a resource detector can be slow, because a cloud detector calls its metadata server, so a signal cancels it as it cancels a slow Init. A failure exits 78 when a *config.Error is in its chain, such as a malformed variable the Builder read, and 1 otherwise. A Builder that returns an SDK with a nil field fails too, and exits 1. In every case Init is never called. Init gets the SDK in Setup.Telemetry, and hands it on to its Services.
Failures are logged through telemetry. The lifecycle logs with the OpenTelemetry Logs API, through Setup.Telemetry.LoggerProvider.Logger("github.com/z5labs/humus"): its own records, serving, shutting down and stopped, at INFO, and every failure after the telemetry is built at ERROR, one record per error, so an operator sees them in the same log stream as everything else. humus has no logging bridge of its own. Standard error still gets what telemetry cannot report itself:
a failure to build telemetry, and a malformed lifecycle setting, which come before there is any telemetry; export errors, each on one line starting with telemetry: . Run sets OpenTelemetry’s process-wide error handler to write them there, because a failing exporter cannot report its own failure; a failure to shut telemetry down. Telemetry shuts down last: after the OnStop functions, or after a failed Init and its OnStop functions. So the spans and logs that record a slow or failed shutdown are still exported. Its context keeps the root context’s values but not its cancellation, and it is separate from the grace period: telemetry.New bounds it with Settings.ShutdownTimeout. A failure to shut telemetry down is joined into the cause of the exit status, and it turns an exit 0 into 1.
Settings Variable Default Meaning HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD App.ShutdownGracePeriod bounds the whole shutdown: every Service’s Shutdown and every OnStop function share it. A time.ParseDuration string, such as 30s, that must be positive. HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY App.DrainDelay the pause between shutdown starting and Shutdown being called on the Services. A time.ParseDuration string, such as 5s, that must not be negative; 0s means no pause. These are the only variables the lifecycle reads, and the root package is the one place humus reads them. Each value is checked after its default, so a bad default fails the same way as a bad variable: an App whose ShutdownGracePeriod is zero, run without HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD, exits 78 with config HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD: must be positive. When both values are bad, both are reported, one line each.
Exit codes Code When Cause 0 a signal stopped the App and it shut down in time the signal 0 a Service returned nil on its own, and the App shut down in time none 1 (humus.ExitFailure) the telemetry could not be built, or its SDK has a nil field the error 1 (humus.ExitFailure) Init, a Service, a Service’s Shutdown, an OnStop function or the telemetry’s shutdown failed every error, joined 1 (humus.ExitFailure) the shutdown ran past the grace period a *humus.GracePeriodError 2 never set by humus: Go’s exit status for an unrecovered panic 78 (humus.ExitConfig) a setting is missing or malformed, including a config value read by the telemetry Builder or by Init a *config.Error in the chain 78 is EX_CONFIG from sysexits.h. It tells an operator “fix the configuration” apart from “the service failed”. Everything else that fails exits 1, and a test tells those failures apart by their cause: errors.AsType[*config.Error] for a config error, and errors.AsType[*humus.GracePeriodError] for a shutdown that ran out of time. A flag usage error is an Init failure and exits 1.
Testing a whole App An App runs whole inside a test. bedrocktest hands it a fake process, whose arguments and environment the test sets, whose output the test reads, and to which the test sends fake signals; and testing/synctest runs it in fake time, so a five-second drain delay passes at once and is measured exactly. The lifecycle’s own tests run it with fake Services:
type fakeService struct { serve func(ctx context.Context) error shutdown func(ctx context.Context) error mu sync.Mutex shutdownCalls int } func (s *fakeService) Serve(ctx context.Context) error { if s.serve == nil { <-ctx.Done() return nil } return s.serve(ctx) } func (s *fakeService) Shutdown(ctx context.Context) error { s.mu.Lock() s.shutdownCalls++ s.mu.Unlock() if s.shutdown == nil { return nil } return s.shutdown(ctx) } This test runs an App with an HTTP-like Service and a consumer through a whole lifecycle, from SIGTERM to the OnStop functions:
func TestApp_Run_a_whole_App(t *testing.T) { synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { // api keeps serving until Shutdown, as an HTTP server does. stopped := make(chan struct{}) var shutdownAt time.Time api := &fakeService{ serve: func(context.Context) error { <-stopped return nil }, shutdown: func(context.Context) error { shutdownAt = time.Now() close(stopped) return nil }, } // consumer stops as soon as Serve's context is done, as a queue // consumer does. var consumerStoppedAt time.Time consumer := &fakeService{serve: func(ctx context.Context) error { <-ctx.Done() consumerStoppedAt = time.Now() return nil }} var poolClosedAt time.Time app := humus.App{ Host: humus.OSHost(), // the fake Services never use it ShutdownGracePeriod: 10 * time.Second, DrainDelay: 5 * time.Second, Telemetry: telemetry.NoopBuilder, Init: func(_ context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { s.OnStop(func(context.Context) error { poolClosedAt = time.Now() return nil }) return []humus.Service{api, consumer}, nil }, } p := bedrocktest.NewProcess(t) status := make(chan bedrock.ExitStatus, 1) go func() { status <- app.Run(t.Context(), p.Process()) }() <-p.Notified(syscall.SIGTERM) sigterm := time.Now() p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM) st := <-status if st.Code() != 0 { t.Errorf("code = %d, want 0: %v", st.Code(), st.Cause()) } if !errors.Is(st.Cause(), context.Canceled) { t.Errorf("cause = %v, want the signal", st.Cause()) } if got := consumerStoppedAt.Sub(sigterm); got != 0 { t.Errorf("consumer stopped %s after SIGTERM, want at once", got) } if got := shutdownAt.Sub(sigterm); got != 5*time.Second { t.Errorf("Shutdown called %s after SIGTERM, want after the 5s drain delay", got) } if api.calls() != 1 || consumer.calls() != 1 { t.Errorf("Shutdown called %d and %d times, want once each", api.calls(), consumer.calls()) } if poolClosedAt.IsZero() || poolClosedAt.Before(shutdownAt) { t.Errorf("OnStop ran at %v, want it after Shutdown at %v", poolClosedAt, shutdownAt) } if got := p.Stderr(); got != "" { t.Errorf("stderr = %q, want nothing", got) } }) } synctest reports a deadlock when a goroutine the App started outlives the test body, which makes it a leak detector for Services. For an HTTP Service the cost is that handlers must honour r.Context(), because a handler that ignores it after the server force-closes the connection outlives the test.
Testing a humus App runs Apps that serve real HTTP, on a humustest Host whose network and filesystem the test controls.
Ambient leaks Some dependencies read the real process behind an App’s back, so they reach around the bedrock.Process and the Host an App is given, and a test can neither control nor see what they read. Avoid them, or configure them explicitly from Setup:
pgx reads the real process. pgx.ParseConfig and pgxpool.ParseConfig take every setting the connection string leaves out from PGHOST, PGUSER, PGPASSWORD and the other PG* variables of the real environment, and default the user to the OS user. They read the password file that PGPASSFILE names, or ~/.pgpass, from the real disk and use it when the connection string sets no password, and they pick up client certificates from ~/.postgresql. The config they return dials the real network: set cfg.ConnConfig.DialFunc = s.Host.Dial before opening the pool. Its LookupFunc still resolves host names with the real resolver. flag.CommandLine and flag.ExitOnError read os.Args and exit the process. Parse p.Args[1:] with a flag.FlagSet of your own, using flag.ContinueOnError. An exec.Cmd with a nil Env inherits the real environment. Build its Env from the keys you know, reading each through p.Environment. http.ProxyFromEnvironment, the Proxy of http.DefaultTransport, reads the proxy variables of the real environment, and http.DefaultClient dials the real network rather than through Host.Dial. slog.Default writes to the real standard error unless it is replaced, and replacing it is process-wide state. OpenTelemetry’s process-wide error handler, which Run sets. In a process with several Apps, the last App to start gets every App’s export errors, so a test that asserts on export errors does not run in parallel. OpenTelemetry’s internal logger, which writes its own errors to the real standard error. OTEL_GO_X_*, OpenTelemetry’s experimental features, which the SDK reads from the real environment. Any resource detector the end user opts into in Settings.ResourceOptions, which reads the real host, such as /etc, /proc and cgroups, or dials a metadata server rather than through Host.Dial. flag, exec.Cmd, http.ProxyFromEnvironment and slog.Default are on bedrock’s own list. A dependency found reading the real process belongs on this list.

body:
humus packages are configured with plain Go values. They read no environment variables, define no variable names and read no files on your behalf. Every value is sourced in your own Init, with whatever names and formats your service already uses: an environment variable called READ_TIMEOUT or MYSVC_HTTP_READ_TIMEOUT, a duration written 5s, a file of PEM, a flag. The usual tool is bedrock’s config package, and this page uses it throughout.
A framework that defined variable names would have to teach them, keep them consistent and document them twice. With Go values, godoc is the only documentation of a package’s settings, and a service’s variables are whatever its team chooses.
The design behind everything on this page is in the configuration revision of Proposal: configuration for humus apps.
What a package with settings exports Every humus package with settings exports the same three things:
a Settings struct, whose fields are plain values; DefaultSettings(), which returns the package’s defaults; a check function, Check<Field>, for each field that has a valid range. A zero field means zero, never “use the default”. A package’s defaults are the values DefaultSettings returns, and nothing else: a field left at zero is checked, and used, as zero. This keeps zero meaningful, as it is for net/http’s timeouts, where a zero ReadTimeout means no timeout.
The godoc of each field gives its default, its valid range and its meaning, and names its check. A check is a func(T) error. Its error says what is wrong, such as must not be negative, and does not name the field: whatever reads the value adds the name.
The samples on this page use a stand-in, declared in the root package’s tests in the shape every package gives it. The telemetry package’s Settings has the same shape, and Telemetry sources it with the same pattern, in the App’s telemetry Builder rather than in Init:
// Settings configures a Greeter. Every field is a plain value, and a field's // zero value means zero, never "use the default". type Settings struct { // Greeting is what the Greeter says. Default "hello". Greeting string // ReadTimeout bounds reading a whole request. Default 5s. Zero means // no timeout. Must not be negative; checked by CheckReadTimeout. ReadTimeout time.Duration // MaxConns is how many connections the Greeter serves at once. // Default 100. Must be positive; checked by CheckMaxConns. MaxConns int } // DefaultSettings returns the defaults of a Greeter. func DefaultSettings() Settings { return Settings{ Greeting: "hello", ReadTimeout: 5 * time.Second, MaxConns: 100, } } // CheckReadTimeout reports why d is not a valid ReadTimeout, or nil if it // is. func CheckReadTimeout(d time.Duration) error { if d < 0 { return errors.New("must not be negative") } return nil } // CheckMaxConns reports why n is not a valid MaxConns, or nil if it is. func CheckMaxConns(n int) error { if n <= 0 { return errors.New("must be positive") } return nil } In a real service these come from the package, as httpserver.Settings, httpserver.DefaultSettings() and httpserver.CheckReadTimeout, and you never copy a range out of godoc.
Sourcing Settings in Init Init reads the package’s Settings with config.Struct. Each field is one config.Value chain: where the value comes from, how it is parsed, .Default with the field of DefaultSettings(), and then the package’s check, chained with .Validate:
func GreeterInit(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { d := DefaultSettings() env := func(name string) config.Value[string] { return config.Env(s.Process.Environment, name) } settings, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) Settings { return Settings{ // The file is read as part of the setting, so a missing file // is a config error named after the variable. Greeting: r.Get(env("GREETING_FILE").Parse(readFile(s.Host.FS)).Default(d.Greeting)), ReadTimeout: r.Get(env("READ_TIMEOUT").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(d.ReadTimeout).Validate(CheckReadTimeout)), MaxConns: r.Get(env("MAX_CONNS").Parse(strconv.Atoi).Default(d.MaxConns).Validate(CheckMaxConns)), } }).Read(ctx) if err != nil { return nil, err // exit 78: every bad variable, one line each } g, err := NewGreeter(settings, s.Process.Stdout) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{g}, nil } The check goes after .Default, and the order matters for two reasons:
The default is checked too. A value that is not set is never checked, so a check chained before .Default would let a bad default through. Chained after it, a bad default fails exactly as a bad variable does. The error names the variable. A check in a field’s chain fails under that value’s name, so the error says READ_TIMEOUT, which is what an operator sets. A check on the whole struct could only name the field, ReadTimeout, which no operator sets. config.Struct attempts every Get, even after one has failed, so a misconfigured service reports all of its problems in one error rather than one per restart. Read every value through the Process and the Host in Setup, never through package os, so that the whole App runs in a test.
Reading a file A setting that names a file reads the file inside the field’s chain. Here GREETING_FILE is parsed by readFile, which opens the file through s.Host.FS:
// readFile returns a parser for config.Value.Parse that reads the whole // file a variable names, through fsys. func readFile(fsys humus.FS) func(name string) (string, error) { return func(name string) (string, error) { f, err := fsys.Open(name) if err != nil { return "", err } defer func() { _ = f.Close() }() b, err := io.ReadAll(f) return string(b), err } } Because the file is read as part of the setting, a missing or unreadable file is a config error named after its variable, and it exits 78 with the rest. humus.FS has no ReadFile: a helper this small is your code, not humus’s API, and it stays unexported. The same goes for decoding: a package takes a decoded value, such as a *tls.Config, never a path or a file’s contents, so how a certificate is stored and encoded is yours to decide. A further .Parse in the chain does the decoding.
How a bad value fails A bad value renders as config <variable>: <cause>. With READ_TIMEOUT=-5s and MAX_CONNS=lots, the App above logs both at ERROR through its telemetry, in one record of two lines, and exits 78:
init: config READ_TIMEOUT: must not be negative config MAX_CONNS: strconv.Atoi: parsing "lots": invalid syntax The lifecycle wraps the error Init returns once, as init: <error>, and logs it as it renders. config.Struct joins its failures with errors.Join, which renders one line per failure, so only the first line carries the init: prefix. Every line that names a bad variable starts config , prefix or not, and that is the word to search for.
And with GREETING_FILE naming a file that does not exist:
init: config GREETING_FILE: openat etc/greeter/greeting.txt: no such file or directory The cause is whatever the Host’s FS returned. This output is from the example, on a humustest Host, whose FS opens files through an os.Root, hence openat. On humus.OSHost() the same file fails with open <path>: no such file or directory.
Every error a config.Value returns is a *config.Error. When one is in the chain of the error Init returns, the App exits 78 (humus.ExitConfig, EX_CONFIG from sysexits.h), which tells an operator “fix the configuration” apart from “the service failed”. errors.AsType[*config.Error] finds the first bad variable in the chain, which is READ_TIMEOUT in the run above. A test that checks every bad variable walks the joined error, whose Unwrap() []error returns one *config.Error per variable, or compares the whole of the record the App logged. The lifecycle’s exit codes list the rest.
Building Settings in code config is a convenience, not a requirement. Settings can come from flags, a YAML file, or plain code:
settings := DefaultSettings() settings.ReadTimeout = -time.Second settings.MaxConns = 0 _, err := NewGreeter(settings, io.Discard) fmt.Println(err) A Settings built this way never passes through a check in a config chain, so the package’s constructor runs every check itself. It reports every bad field in one error, naming each field rather than a variable:
ReadTimeout: must not be negative MaxConns: must be positive The constructor of the stand-in shows the shape:
func NewGreeter(s Settings, out io.Writer) (*Greeter, error) { var errs []error if err := CheckReadTimeout(s.ReadTimeout); err != nil { errs = append(errs, fmt.Errorf("ReadTimeout: %w", err)) } if err := CheckMaxConns(s.MaxConns); err != nil { errs = append(errs, fmt.Errorf("MaxConns: %w", err)) } if err := errors.Join(errs...); err != nil { return nil, err } return &Greeter{settings: s, out: out}, nil } Its error is not a *config.Error, so an Init that returns it exits 1. A service that sources its settings with config and chains each check never reaches it: the bad value has already exited 78, named after its variable.
The variables humus reads humus reads exactly two variables, both in the lifecycle: HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD and HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY. humus.App.Run reads them before it calls Init, with defaults from App’s own fields, and checks each after its default, as on this page. The lifecycle’s settings describes them. That is the one exception to “humus defines no variable names”, and no humus package adds another. The telemetry package reads no OTEL_* variable either: a Builder that wants them maps them onto telemetry.Settings itself, as Telemetry shows.
Logging and secrets humus logs no settings, and it does not redact any. Whether to log the values a service started with, which ones, and how to hide a secret among them are your decisions. Init is given the same Process and Host that humus has, so it can log anything it wants, environment variables included, to s.Process.Stderr or to a logger of its own.
What humus does log is the error Init returns, through the App’s telemetry, and a parse error often quotes the value it could not parse: parsing "lots" above. A malformed secret, such as a token in the wrong format or a key that does not decode, would be logged the same way. Keeping a secret out of that error is part of the same choice: give the secret’s chain a parser of your own whose error says what is wrong without quoting the input.
Testing it Settings are tested by running the whole App: a bedrocktest Process with the variables set, and a humustest Host with the files the settings name. One of the root package’s examples runs the App above this way:
h := humustest.NewHost(t, humustest.WithFiles(files)) tel := humustest.NewTelemetry() app := humus.App{ Host: h.Host(), ShutdownGracePeriod: 10 * time.Second, Telemetry: tel.Builder(), Init: GreeterInit, } fp := bedrocktest.NewProcess(t, bedrocktest.WithEnv(env)) status := app.Run(context.Background(), fp.Process()) Telemetry is humustest.Telemetry’s Builder, so the example prints the errors the App logged from the recorder’s Logs().
ShutdownGracePeriod is the lifecycle’s own setting, not the Greeter’s. The grace period must be positive and humus has no default of its own, so an App sets it unless HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD is always set; left at zero, the App would exit 78 naming that variable before Init ran.
A relative name given to the humustest Host’s FS is relative to the test’s temp directory, and an absolute one, from h.Path, must be inside it, so a setting naming a file never reaches the real disk. Testing a humus App covers the Host in full.
description: How a humus service's settings get their values: humus packages take plain Go values, and the service's Init sources each one, usually with bedrock's config package, so that a bad value fails startup with exit 78 and an error naming the variable.

title: Configuring a humus service

body:
A humus App builds its OpenTelemetry providers before Init, hands them to Init as one value, logs through them, and shuts them down last. The telemetry package builds them from a plain Settings value, and the service’s own Builder sources that value, the same way Init sources any other package’s settings.
The design behind everything on this page is in Proposal: OpenTelemetry without globals, Revision 2. The lifecycle describes when the App builds its telemetry and shuts it down.
Where the providers come from A Service gets its providers from s.Telemetry, the telemetry.SDK in the Setup that Init is given. An SDK is a plain struct: a TracerProvider, a MeterProvider, a LoggerProvider, a Propagator, and the Shutdown that the App calls once it has stopped. Neither Init nor a Service calls Shutdown.
humus never reads or sets OpenTelemetry’s global providers or its global propagator, and it never replaces slog.Default. Every humus package takes an SDK, and third-party instrumentation is handed its providers explicitly: otelhttp’s options, grpc’s stats/opentelemetry options, and otelslog.WithLoggerProvider. This Init takes its Service’s tracer and logger from s.Telemetry:
func CartsInit(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { tracer := s.Telemetry.TracerProvider.Tracer("carts") logger := otelslog.NewLogger("carts", otelslog.WithLoggerProvider(s.Telemetry.LoggerProvider)) return []humus.Service{&cartJob{tracer: tracer, logger: logger}}, nil } A library that reads only the global providers can be given them: set them in Init, from s.Telemetry. That is your decision and your global state, not humus’s. The one piece of global state humus does set is OpenTelemetry’s error handler.
Writing the Builder App.Telemetry is a telemetry.Builder, and the end user writes it. It is given the context a signal cancels, the bedrock.Process and the Host’s Dial, and it does three things:
sources telemetry.Settings from p.Environment with config.Struct, starting from telemetry.DefaultSettings(); chains each field’s check after its default, so a bad default fails as a bad variable does, and the error names the variable; calls telemetry.New with the Settings, dial and p.Stdout. Configuring a humus service explains the pattern. This Builder keeps the OpenTelemetry specification’s variable names, but the names are yours to choose:
func buildCartsTelemetry(ctx context.Context, p bedrock.Process, dial telemetry.Dialer) (telemetry.SDK, error) { d := telemetry.DefaultSettings() env := func(name string) config.Value[string] { return config.Env(p.Environment, name) } exporter := func(name string, def telemetry.Exporter) config.Value[telemetry.Exporter] { return env(name). Map(func(s string) telemetry.Exporter { return telemetry.Exporter(s) }). Default(def). Validate(telemetry.CheckExporter) } s, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) telemetry.Settings { s := d s.Disabled = r.Get(env("OTEL_SDK_DISABLED").Parse(strconv.ParseBool).Default(d.Disabled)) s.ServiceName = r.Get(env("OTEL_SERVICE_NAME").Default("carts").Validate(telemetry.CheckServiceName)) s.Traces = r.Get(exporter("OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER", d.Traces)) s.Metrics = r.Get(exporter("OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER", d.Metrics)) s.Logs = r.Get(exporter("OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER", d.Logs)) return s }).Read(ctx) if err != nil { return telemetry.SDK{}, err // exit 78: every bad variable, one line each } return telemetry.New(ctx, s, dial, p.Stdout) } s := d starts from every default, so a field the Builder does not source, such as LogLevel here, keeps its default. DefaultSettings cannot see the process, so it names the service unknown_service. The Builder names it.
With OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=zipkin, this App never calls Init. It writes the error to standard error, because it has no telemetry yet to log it through, and exits 78:
build telemetry: config OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER: "zipkin" is not one of none, console or otlp telemetry.New runs every check too, so a Settings built in code is checked as well. Its error names each bad field, such as telemetry: Settings.Traces: "zipkin" is not one of none, console or otlp, and an App whose Builder returns it exits 1, not 78: the bad value came from code, not from a variable.
A Builder that needs something Settings does not cover, such as a metric view or a Prometheus reader, builds the SDK value itself, Shutdown included. humustest’s recorder is built that way.
Settings telemetry.Settings follows the shape every humus package’s settings take: plain values, DefaultSettings(), and a check for each field with a valid range. A zero field means zero, never “use the default”.
Field Default Valid Check Spec variable Disabled false any OTEL_SDK_DISABLED ServiceName "unknown_service" not empty CheckServiceName OTEL_SERVICE_NAME ResourceOptions none, so no detector runs any OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES, as resource.WithAttributes Traces ExporterNone none, console, otlp CheckExporter OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER Metrics ExporterNone none, console, otlp CheckExporter OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER Logs ExporterConsole none, console, otlp CheckExporter OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER OTLP.Endpoint "localhost:4317" host:port, with a port from 1 to 65535 CheckOTLPEndpoint OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, which is a URL in the spec OTLP.Protocol ProtocolGRPC grpc, http/protobuf CheckOTLPProtocol OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL OTLP.Headers none any OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS OTLP.TLS nil, which means plaintext any OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_CERTIFICATE and the related variables OTLP.Timeout 10s positive CheckOTLPTimeout OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT Sampler sdktrace.ParentBased(sdktrace.AlwaysSample()) not nil CheckSampler OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER and OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG LogLevel log.SeverityInfo log.SeverityTrace1 to log.SeverityFatal4 CheckLogLevel none ShutdownTimeout 5s positive CheckShutdownTimeout none The godoc of each field is the reference; the table is its summary. The OTLP fields are checked even when no signal is exported over OTLP. The OTLP exporters dial the collector through the Dialer the Builder is given, which is the Host’s Dial, and over http/protobuf each signal is sent to its spec path: /v1/traces, /v1/metrics and /v1/logs.
humus reads none of these variables. The last column names the specification’s variable with the same meaning, for a Builder that wants to stay compatible with it, as the one above does. It is not a variable humus reads: there is no FromEnvironment and no parser for the specification’s formats. So a platform that injects OTEL_* variables, such as the OpenTelemetry Operator, has no effect on an App unless its Builder reads them.
telemetry.New gives the OpenTelemetry SDK every option explicitly, at the SDK’s own default where Settings has no field, so the SDK’s own reads of the real environment are overridden too. The few that still take effect, such as OTEL_GO_X_*, are listed under the lifecycle’s ambient leaks.
The defaults With DefaultSettings():
Logs are written to standard output, as one line of JSON per record, in the console log format. Traces are not exported, but spans still get IDs. At ExporterNone, the TracerProvider is still the SDK’s, built with the Sampler and the resource but with no span processor. Every span gets a real trace ID and span ID, and a record logged in it carries them, but nothing is exported. That is the usual local setup: the logs on standard output can be grouped by request without running a collector. Metrics are a no-op. Sampling is the same with or without an exporter: the TracerProvider keeps the configured Sampler, so the sampled flag passed on to downstream services does not change when Traces does.
Traces at none have a cost in the middle of a shared trace. A service at none in a traced call chain passes on span IDs that no backend ever receives. The trace ID is still the caller’s, so the trace holds together, but the downstream spans point to a parent that is missing. A service that takes part in a traced system sets Traces to otlp.
The console log format At ExporterConsole, each log record is written to standard output as one line of JSON, terminated by a newline:
{"timestamp":"2026-10-16T06:56:32.447829601Z","severity_text":"INFO","severity_number":9,"body":"cart created","trace_id":"e2f668b6c06f2de82e61e2517c2d7a07","span_id":"ff25eb972a5557d5","trace_flags":"01","scope":"carts","attributes":{"cart.id":"c-123"}} This format is part of humus’s API. Renaming, reordering, adding or removing a key, or encoding a value differently, is a breaking change. It is humus’s own, written by an exporter of the telemetry package, so upgrading OpenTelemetry does not change it. A golden test pins it byte for byte.
The keys are always written in this order, and each one only when the record has what it holds:
Key Value Present timestamp the record’s timestamp or, when that is unset, its observed timestamp, in UTC, as RFC 3339 with exactly nine fractional digits always severity_text the record’s severity text or, when that is empty, the short name of its severity number: TRACE, TRACE2, …, INFO, …, FATAL4 when the severity number is set, that is when it is one of OpenTelemetry’s severities 1 to 24 severity_number the record’s OpenTelemetry severity number, 1 to 24, for filtering by threshold under the same condition as severity_text event_name the record’s event name when it is not empty body the record’s body, encoded as below when the body is set trace_id, span_id, trace_flags the trace context of the span the record was logged in, as lowercase hex: 32, 16 and 2 digits only when the record has a valid span context, one whose trace ID and span ID are both non-zero scope the name of the record’s instrumentation scope, the name its logger was created with always, and empty when that name is attributes an object whose keys are the attribute keys, in the record’s order when the record has at least one attribute The keys are the OpenTelemetry log data model’s field names, in snake case. The trace context keys follow OpenTelemetry’s stable specification for trace context in non-OTLP log formats, so a log pipeline links a line to its trace by the names the specification gives. A record logged outside a span has none of the three, rather than zeros, because a zero ID would point to a trace that does not exist.
The record’s resource is never written: OTLP carries the resource, and on standard output whatever collects the logs, such as a Kubernetes log agent, adds its own metadata. Neither is its count of dropped attributes.
A body and an attribute value are encoded the same way:
a string as a JSON string, a bool as true or false, and an integer as a JSON number; a finite float as a JSON number, and NaN and the infinities as the strings "NaN", "+Inf" and "-Inf", so that every line is valid JSON; bytes as a string holding their standard, padded base64 encoding; a slice, typed slices included, as an array, and a map as an object with its keys sorted by their bytes, each element encoded by these rules; an empty value as null, as an attribute’s value or inside a slice or map. An empty body is not written at all. An attribute key a record holds more than once, which happens only when its logger provider allows duplicate keys, is written once for each value, and so is a key a map holds more than once. Strings are escaped as JSON requires and no further: <, > and & are written as they are. Invalid UTF-8 is replaced by U+FFFD.
The telemetry package doc is the specification of the format, and this section its summary.
Traces and metrics at ExporterConsole are written by OpenTelemetry’s stdouttrace and stdoutmetric. They are for debugging, and humus makes no promise about their format.
Trace context in logs telemetry.SDK exposes a LoggerProvider, not a logger: humus has no logging bridge of its own. Use the OpenTelemetry Logs API directly, or bridge the LoggerProvider to the logging library you already use, such as otelslog for log/slog, as CartsInit above does.
A record carries a trace context only when the log call is given the span’s context. With otelslog, that means InfoContext, not Info: Info logs with context.Background(), so its record has no trace fields, whatever exporter it goes to. In a handler, pass the request’s context, r.Context(). This Service logs both ways inside one span:
func (j *cartJob) Serve(ctx context.Context) error { ctx, span := j.tracer.Start(ctx, "create cart") defer span.End() // InfoContext, not Info: the record takes its trace context from ctx, // so it carries the span's trace_id and span_id. j.logger.InfoContext(ctx, "cart created", slog.String("cart.id", "c-123")) // Info logs with context.Background(), so this record has no trace // context, even though it is logged inside the span. j.logger.Info("cart created, untraced") return nil } With the defaults, the first line on standard output has trace_id, span_id and trace_flags, and the second has none of them.
Other settings LogLevel is the lowest severity the LoggerProvider exports, as an OpenTelemetry severity rather than a slog.Level. It is applied in the provider: its loggers’ Enabled reports false below it, so a bridge that asks Enabled before building a record, as otelslog’s handler does, skips a filtered record at no cost, and a record below it is dropped either way. A record with no severity, log.SeverityUndefined, is not on the scale and is kept. ShutdownTimeout bounds SDK.Shutdown: every provider is flushed and stopped within it. The App shuts telemetry down after the OnStop functions, separately from the grace period and with a context that a cancelled root context does not cancel, so ShutdownTimeout is what bounds it. Disabled is the counterpart of OTEL_SDK_DISABLED. telemetry.New ignores every other field and returns telemetry.Noop(), building and dialling nothing. The propagator stays W3C trace context plus baggage, because the specification disables signals, not propagation, so a request’s trace passes through. Unlike traces at none, a disabled SDK makes no IDs of its own: it passes on the span context a request brought. Resource detectors are opt-in. The resource is ServiceName plus whatever ResourceOptions adds, and by default no detector runs, so the resource is service.name alone. A detector, such as resource.WithHost() or a contrib cloud detector, reads the real host rather than the humus.Host: the host, process and container detectors read /etc, /proc and cgroups, and a cloud detector dials its metadata server. Opt in knowingly. ServiceName wins over a service.name any detector finds. telemetry.New fails if any option fails, even partly, and some detectors fail where their attribute cannot be found: resource.WithProcess includes the process owner, which cannot be looked up in an image without a passwd entry for its user. Opt in to the detectors whose attributes the environment has, such as resource.WithProcessPID, rather than to a group of them. Testing A test that asserts on what an App emits runs it with humustest.NewTelemetry()’s Builder in place of the one production uses. The recorder uses the real OpenTelemetry SDK with in-memory exporters, records every severity, samples every span, starts no goroutine, so it works under synctest, and keeps what it recorded after the App has shut it down:
h := humustest.NewHost(t) tel := humustest.NewTelemetry() app := humus.App{ Host: h.Host(), ShutdownGracePeriod: 10 * time.Second, Telemetry: tel.Builder(), Init: CartsInit, } fp := bedrocktest.NewProcess(t) status := app.Run(context.Background(), fp.Process()) Once the App has exited, tel.Spans(), tel.Metrics(ctx) and tel.Logs() return what it emitted. Here they show the span create cart, and that the record logged with InfoContext is in it:
span := tel.Spans()[0] fmt.Println("span:", span.Name()) for _, r := range tel.Logs() { if r.InstrumentationScope().Name != "carts" { continue // the lifecycle's own records } inSpan := r.TraceID() == span.SpanContext().TraceID() && r.SpanID() == span.SpanContext().SpanID() fmt.Printf("logged %s: %s, in the span: %t\n", r.SeverityText(), r.Body().AsString(), inSpan) } The lifecycle’s own records, serving, shutting down, stopped and every failure after the telemetry is built, are in tel.Logs() too, under the scope github.com/z5labs/humus.
A test that does not assert on telemetry uses telemetry.NoopBuilder, whose SDK discards everything. A test of the Builder itself runs the App with it and a bedrocktest Process whose environment the test sets, and reads standard output, where the console logs go, and standard error, where a bad variable goes. The root package’s examples run the Builder above that way.
Testing a humus App covers the rest of a whole-App test.
The error handler Telemetry cannot report its own failure: a failing OTLP log exporter would swallow the errors about itself, and each error would queue another record bound to fail. So once the SDK is built, Run sets OpenTelemetry’s process-wide error handler to one that writes each export error to the Process’s standard error, as one line starting with telemetry: . Export errors join the failures standard error already gets, those that come before there is any telemetry or that are about telemetry itself: a failure to build or shut it down, and a malformed lifecycle setting.
This is the one piece of OpenTelemetry’s global state humus sets, and its one call to otel.SetErrorHandler. Being process-wide, it has two consequences:
In a process that runs several Apps, the last App to start gets every App’s export errors. So a test that asserts on export errors does not run in parallel with another App. An end user who wants a different handler sets it in Init, which runs after Run has set its own. OpenTelemetry’s internal logger is separate from the handler, and writes its own errors to the real standard error. It is on the lifecycle’s list of ambient leaks.

title: Telemetry

body:
A humus App runs whole inside a test. Two packages make that possible, and a whole-App test imports both:
bedrocktest supplies the process the App runs on: its arguments and environment, which the test sets, its output, which the test reads, and its signals, which the test sends. bedrocktest.Start runs an App on a new process and hands back the process and a channel for the App’s exit status. humustest supplies what a humus App needs beyond the process: a Host, whose in-memory network the App listens on and the test dials, and whose filesystem is confined to the test’s own temp directory; a certificate authority, NewCA, generated for each test; and TestService, the contract every Service must pass. The network opens no real socket and starts no goroutines, so the App runs in a testing/synctest bubble. It needs no real environment, no real time and no file outside the test’s temp directory.
The design behind everything on this page is in Proposal: humustest. Recording an App’s telemetry in a test, with humustest.NewTelemetry(), is covered on the Telemetry page.
A whole-App test This test runs an App whose Service serves HTTP on :8080, sends it a request and stops it with SIGTERM:
func TestApp_Run_HTTP_a_whole_App_on_a_test_Host(t *testing.T) { synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { h := humustest.NewHost(t) hello := http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, _ *http.Request) { _, _ = io.WriteString(w, "hello") }) p, status := bedrocktest.Start(t, httpApp(h, hello)) // Wait until every goroutine in the bubble is blocked, which // includes the App blocked in Accept on :8080. synctest.Wait() resp, err := h.HTTPClient().Get("http://localhost:8080/") if err != nil { t.Fatal(err) } b, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body) _ = resp.Body.Close() if err != nil { t.Fatal(err) } if string(b) != "hello" { t.Errorf("body = %q, want hello", b) } p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM) st := <-status if st.Code() != 0 { t.Errorf("code = %d, want 0: %v", st.Code(), st.Cause()) } requireSignalCause(t, st.Cause()) requireRefused(t, h, "localhost:8080") }) } httpApp builds the App on the Host. Its Host field is h.Host(), the humus.Host of the test Host, just as a test passes p.Process() where a bedrock.Process is wanted:
func httpApp(h *humustest.Host, handler http.Handler, more ...humus.Service) humus.App { return humus.App{ Host: h.Host(), ShutdownGracePeriod: 10 * time.Second, Telemetry: telemetry.NoopBuilder, Init: func(_ context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { return append([]humus.Service{newHTTPService(s, ":8080", handler)}, more...), nil }, } } The Service listens through s.Host.Listen, never through net.Listen, so it listens on the test Host. h.HTTPClient() is an http.Client that dials the Host, with keep-alives off so that no idle connection outlives a request.
Build the Host, and a CA, inside the bubble that uses them, with the bubble’s t, so that everything they make belongs to that bubble.
The network The Host’s network follows the rules of a real one.
A name and port can be held once. A listener on every name, an empty host, 0.0.0.0 or ::, conflicts with any other listener on its port. A second Listen on a held name and port fails with EADDRINUSE. Names are compared as written and never resolved. localhost and 127.0.0.1 are different names, so a client dials the name a Service listens on, or the Service listens on every name, as :8080 does above. h := humustest.NewHost(t) ln, err := h.Listen("tcp", "localhost:8080") if err != nil { fmt.Println(err) return } defer func() { _ = ln.Close() }() go func() { conn, err := ln.Accept() if err != nil { return } defer func() { _ = conn.Close() }() _, _ = io.WriteString(conn, "hello from localhost:8080") }() conn, err := h.Dial(context.Background(), "tcp", "localhost:8080") if err != nil { fmt.Println(err) return } defer func() { _ = conn.Close() }() b, err := io.ReadAll(conn) if err != nil { fmt.Println(err) return } fmt.Println(string(b)) _, err = h.Dial(context.Background(), "tcp", "127.0.0.1:8080") fmt.Println("127.0.0.1:8080 refused:", errors.Is(err, syscall.ECONNREFUSED)) // Output: // hello from localhost:8080 // 127.0.0.1:8080 refused: true Waiting for a listener Dial refuses rather than waits. A Dial with no listener fails at once with ECONNREFUSED, as a real dial does. A test that dials before the App listens has dialled too early, and waiting for a listener would hide that, or turn it into a synctest deadlock report that doesn’t name the cause.
So a test waits for the listener itself, before it dials, in one of two ways:
Inside a synctest bubble, synctest.Wait(). It returns once every goroutine in the bubble is blocked, which includes the App blocked in Accept. That is what the whole-App test above does. Anywhere, <-h.Listening(address). It waits for one particular listener, and works outside a bubble too. It works like bedrocktest’s Notified: once closed, the channel stays closed. h := humustest.NewHost(t) _, err := h.Dial(context.Background(), "tcp", "localhost:8080") fmt.Println("before Listen, refused:", errors.Is(err, syscall.ECONNREFUSED)) // The goroutine stands in for an App, which listens when it gets to // it. Listening is called first, so the test can't miss the listener. listening := h.Listening("localhost:8080") served := make(chan struct{}) go func() { defer close(served) ln, err := h.Listen("tcp", ":8080") if err != nil { fmt.Println(err) return } defer func() { _ = ln.Close() }() conn, err := ln.Accept() if err != nil { return } defer func() { _ = conn.Close() }() _, _ = io.WriteString(conn, "hello from every name") }() select { case <-listening: case <-served: // Listen failed, and the goroutine said why return } conn, err := h.Dial(context.Background(), "tcp", "localhost:8080") if err != nil { fmt.Println(err) return } defer func() { _ = conn.Close() }() b, err := io.ReadAll(conn) if err != nil { fmt.Println(err) return } fmt.Println(string(b)) <-served // Output: // before Listen, refused: true // hello from every name Files The filesystem is real. NewHost takes a directory from t.TempDir(), which is removed when the test ends, and WithFiles writes the files a test sets up before the App starts. Host.FS opens files with an os.Root on that directory, so .. and symbolic links can’t leave it, and Host.Path gives the absolute path of a file in it to put in a setting:
h := humustest.NewHost(t, humustest.WithFiles(map[string][]byte{ "etc/app/greeting.txt": []byte("hello from a real file"), })) path := h.Path("etc/app/greeting.txt") fmt.Println("absolute:", filepath.IsAbs(path)) f, err := h.FS().Open(path) if err != nil { fmt.Println(err) return } defer func() { _ = f.Close() }() b, err := io.ReadAll(f) if err != nil { fmt.Println(err) return } fmt.Println(string(b)) _, err = h.FS().Open("../outside.txt") fmt.Println("outside the directory refused:", err != nil) // Output: // absolute: true // hello from a real file // outside the directory refused: true Real files are what let libraries that need an *os.File or a path, such as SQLite drivers, archive libraries and programs started with os/exec, keep working in a test. They cost two things:
No injected I/O errors. A test can’t make a write fail with a full disk. Code that needs that test puts an io.Writer seam in its own code. Real ModTime, even inside synctest. A bubble’s clock is fake, and a file’s modification time is not, so code that compares ModTime() with time.Now() needs os.Chtimes in its tests. The App lifecycle explains why FS hands out *os.File.
TLS A test that serves TLS generates what it needs with NewCA, and never uses a fixed key, certificate or password. Each CA, and each certificate it issues with Issue, has a new random key and serial number, and each PKCS12 bundle a new random password. So no secret is ever written into the repository, and nothing is shared between tests.
This App reads its certificate from a PKCS#12 bundle, through its Host, and serves HTTPS. The test writes the bundle with WithFiles, passes its path and password in settings, and trusts the CA through ca.Pool():
func TestApp_Run_HTTPS_with_a_PKCS12_bundle_from_NewCA(t *testing.T) { synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { ca := humustest.NewCA(t) bundle, password := ca.Issue(t, "api.internal").PKCS12(t) h := humustest.NewHost(t, humustest.WithFiles(map[string][]byte{ "etc/tls/server.p12": bundle, })) hello := http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, _ *http.Request) { _, _ = io.WriteString(w, "hello over TLS") }) app := humus.App{ Host: h.Host(), ShutdownGracePeriod: 10 * time.Second, Telemetry: telemetry.NoopBuilder, Init: func(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { cfg, err := tlsFromPKCS12(ctx, s) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{newHTTPSService(s, ":8443", cfg, hello)}, nil }, } p, status := bedrocktest.Start(t, app, bedrocktest.WithEnv(map[string]string{ "TLS_PKCS12_FILE": h.Path("etc/tls/server.p12"), "TLS_PKCS12_PASSWORD": password, })) synctest.Wait() client := h.HTTPClient() client.Transport.(*http.Transport).TLSClientConfig = &tls.Config{RootCAs: ca.Pool()} resp, err := client.Get("https://api.internal:8443/") if err != nil { t.Fatal(err) } b, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body) _ = resp.Body.Close() if err != nil { t.Fatal(err) } if string(b) != "hello over TLS" { t.Errorf("body = %q, want hello over TLS", b) } p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM) st := <-status if st.Code() != 0 { t.Errorf("code = %d, want 0: %v", st.Code(), st.Cause()) } if got := p.Stderr(); got != "" { t.Errorf("stderr = %q, want nothing", got) } }) } The setting names are only for illustration; each runtime package names its own. tlsFromPKCS12 opens the bundle through s.Host.FS, so the App reads it from the test’s directory here and from the real disk in production:
func tlsFromPKCS12(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) (*tls.Config, error) { path, err := config.Env(s.Process.Environment, "TLS_PKCS12_FILE").Read(ctx) if err != nil { return nil, err } password, err := config.Env(s.Process.Environment, "TLS_PKCS12_PASSWORD").Read(ctx) if err != nil { return nil, err } f, err := s.Host.FS.Open(path) if err != nil { return nil, err } defer func() { _ = f.Close() }() b, err := io.ReadAll(f) if err != nil { return nil, err } key, leaf, chain, err := pkcs12.DecodeChain(b, password) if err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("decode %s: %w", path, err) } cert := tls.Certificate{Certificate: [][]byte{leaf.Raw}, PrivateKey: key, Leaf: leaf} for _, c := range chain { cert.Certificate = append(cert.Certificate, c.Raw) } return &tls.Config{Certificates: []tls.Certificate{cert}}, nil } h.HTTPClient() returns a new client, with a new *http.Transport, on every call, so setting its TLSClientConfig changes no other client.
A server that takes a tls.Certificate rather than a file serves cert.TLS() instead, and a client that dials the Host itself trusts the CA’s pool:
ca := humustest.NewCA(t) cert := ca.Issue(t, "api.internal") h := humustest.NewHost(t) ln, err := h.Listen("tcp", "api.internal:8443") if err != nil { fmt.Println(err) return } defer func() { _ = ln.Close() }() go func() { conn, err := ln.Accept() if err != nil { return } srv := tls.Server(conn, &tls.Config{Certificates: []tls.Certificate{cert.TLS()}}) defer func() { _ = srv.Close() }() _, _ = io.WriteString(srv, "hello over TLS") }() conn, err := h.Dial(context.Background(), "tcp", "api.internal:8443") if err != nil { fmt.Println(err) return } client := tls.Client(conn, &tls.Config{RootCAs: ca.Pool(), ServerName: "api.internal"}) defer func() { _ = client.Close() }() b, err := io.ReadAll(client) if err != nil { fmt.Println(err) return } fmt.Println(string(b)) fmt.Println("verified for:", client.ConnectionState().PeerCertificates[0].DNSNames) // Output: // hello over TLS // verified for: [api.internal] A connection on the Host’s network is a net.Pipe, which has no buffer. When both ends of a TLS connection close at once, each waits to send its close_notify alert until crypto/tls’s five-second write deadline passes. Inside a synctest bubble that wait takes no time; outside one, it is real.
Checking a Service A package that provides a humus.Service checks it with TestService, from a test of its own:
func TestHTTPService(t *testing.T) { humustest.TestService(t, func(t *testing.T, s *humus.Setup) humus.Service { return newHTTPService(s, ":8080", http.NotFoundHandler()) }) } TestService runs the Service contract against it inside synctest, each rule in a subtest named after it:
Serve returns nil after Shutdown. Shutdown with a context that is already done stops the Service at once, and returns an error that wraps the context’s error. Shutdown is safe before Serve, after Serve has returned on its own, and twice. No goroutine the Service started outlives Serve. The Service must reach the network and the filesystem only through the Setup’s Host. A goroutine blocked on a real socket is one synctest can’t see, and the test then hangs until its timeout.
For package authors Every package proposal, and every package that lands from one, shows in its tests that:
Its App or Service runs whole under synctest with bedrocktest and humustest. No test calls t.Setenv, opens a real socket or touches a file outside its own temp directory, except integration tests behind a build tag. Negative tests assert why something failed — the cause, with errors.Is or errors.AsType — not only the exit code. A test that checks a logged failure reads it from humustest’s telemetry recorder, humustest.Telemetry. Every Service passes humustest.TestService. And one rule for every test, fixture and testdata file:
No secrets. None contains a private key, a certificate, a password or a token, even one made only for tests. A test generates the secrets it needs, such as with humustest.NewCA, so that no copy of a fixed key ends up in a repository or in the test suites copied from it. A negative test that meets the third requirement asserts the cause:
st := <-status if st.Code() != humus.ExitFailure { t.Errorf("code = %d, want %d", st.Code(), humus.ExitFailure) } if !errors.Is(st.Cause(), pkcs12.ErrIncorrectPassword) { t.Errorf("cause = %v, want pkcs12.ErrIncorrectPassword", st.Cause()) } The App lifecycle page lists the dependencies that read the real process behind an App’s back, which a whole-App test can neither control nor see.
description: How to run a whole humus App inside a test with bedrocktest and humustest: under synctest, with no real socket, no file outside the test's temp directory and no secret in the repository.

body:
An opinionated Go framework for building services on bedrock’s process model.
Humus is for HTTP and REST APIs, gRPC services, queue consumers and jobs, with telemetry, health and graceful shutdown built in. Every humus application is a bedrock.App, and its main is func main() { bedrock.Main(app) }.
Humus is being rebuilt Humus is being rebuilt on bedrock’s process model, package by package. The previous code, and the pages that documented it, have been removed: the Builder/Runner code, the YAML configuration, the global telemetry, and the rest, grpc, job, queue and health packages. Each package comes back through its own accepted proposal, and its pages are written here as it lands.
The App lifecycle has landed in the root package: The App lifecycle explains humus.App, which every humus app type is built on. The runtime packages built on it have not landed yet. Configuring a humus service explains how a service’s settings are sourced, Telemetry explains how a service gets its OpenTelemetry providers, and Testing a humus App explains how to run a whole App inside a test with bedrocktest and humustest.
The plan is in the charter, Proposal: humus on the bedrock process model.
Earlier releases, and their package documentation, remain available on pkg.go.dev.
